questions.prompt: Which ASP.NET Core DI lifetime gives one instance per HTTP request?
questions.explanation: Scoped services live for the request's scope (DbContext is the classic example). Transient is a new instance every time it's resolved, even twice in one request; singleton is one for the app's lifetime.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong when a singleton service takes a scoped service, such as a DbContext, in its constructor?
questions.answer: The scoped instance is captured for the app's lifetime (a captive dependency): one DbContext shared by every request and thread
distractors: Nothing: the container hands the singleton a fresh scoped instance on each request
The singleton gets re-created for every request instead
questions.explanation: The singleton is built once, so whatever it was given stays with it. A shared DbContext isn't thread-safe and keeps tracking entities forever. In Development, scope validation throws at startup to catch this; inject IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope per unit of work instead.

questions.prompt: What happens to a request when an ASP.NET Core middleware doesn't call `next()`?
questions.answer: The pipeline short-circuits: later middleware and the endpoint never run, and this middleware's response is sent
distractors: The framework calls next() automatically after the middleware returns
The request fails with a 500 error
Later middleware still runs, but can't change the response
questions.explanation: Middleware forms a chain where each one decides whether to pass the request on. Static files and auth failures short-circuit on purpose; forgetting `await next(context)` does it by accident.

questions.prompt: Which must come first in the middleware pipeline: `UseAuthentication()` or `UseAuthorization()`?
questions.explanation: Authentication works out who the user is (sets HttpContext.User); authorization then decides what they may do. The other way round, authorization sees an anonymous user and rejects everything.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP status code means "no valid credentials, please authenticate", as opposed to 403 "authenticated but not allowed"?
questions.explanation: Despite its name, 401 Unauthorized means unauthenticated. 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are and the answer is still no.

questions.prompt: Which attribute on a controller turns on automatic 400 responses for invalid models and infers `[FromBody]` for complex parameters?
questions.explanation: [ApiController] adds API conventions: ModelState is checked for you (returning a ProblemDetails 400), attribute routing is required, and binding sources are inferred.

questions.prompt: Which interface do you inject to create `HttpClient` instances in ASP.NET Core, so connections are pooled and DNS changes are still picked up?
questions.explanation: IHttpClientFactory (via AddHttpClient) reuses and periodically recycles the underlying handlers. That avoids both socket exhaustion from creating clients per request and stale DNS from one static client living forever.

questions.prompt: What's wrong with `using var client = new HttpClient();` inside every request handler?
questions.answer: Each disposed client leaves its connection in TIME_WAIT, so under load the server runs out of sockets (socket exhaustion)
distractors: Nothing: HttpClient isn't thread-safe, so one per request is the correct pattern
Disposing one HttpClient cancels requests running on the other instances
The using block disposes the client before the response arrives
questions.explanation: HttpClient is designed to be reused and is safe to share across threads. Creating and disposing one per request throws away pooled connections; use IHttpClientFactory or a long-lived client with SocketsHttpHandler.PooledConnectionLifetime.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid `.Result` or `.Wait()` on async calls inside an ASP.NET Core request?
questions.answer: It blocks a thread-pool thread while waiting, so under load the pool starves and throughput collapses
distractors: It deadlocks on every call, because of ASP.NET Core's SynchronizationContext
It's harmless: each request has its own dedicated thread
It makes the async method run twice
questions.explanation: ASP.NET Core has no SynchronizationContext, so the classic UI-style deadlock doesn't happen there. The cost is thread-pool starvation: blocked threads can't serve other requests, and the pool only adds threads slowly.

questions.prompt: Which method maps a minimal API endpoint for HTTP GET, e.g. `app.____("/todos", ...)`?
questions.explanation: Minimal APIs use MapGet, MapPost, MapPut and MapDelete on the WebApplication. `Use...` methods add middleware and `Add...` methods register services.

questions.prompt: Which options interface is registered as scoped and recomputes the options once per request, so edits to appsettings.json show up in the next request?
questions.explanation: IOptions<T> is a singleton read once at startup. IOptionsMonitor<T> is also a singleton but tracks changes (with OnChange callbacks), so it suits singletons; IOptionsSnapshot<T> gives a consistent per-request value.

questions.prompt: With the default configuration sources, which wins when the same key is set in appsettings.json, an environment variable and a command-line argument?
questions.explanation: Sources added later override earlier ones: appsettings.json, then appsettings.{Environment}.json, user secrets (in Development), environment variables, and finally command-line arguments.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism lets JavaScript on one origin call your API on another origin, controlled by response headers such as `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`?
questions.explanation: Browsers block cross-origin requests unless the server opts in with CORS headers (UseCors in ASP.NET Core). CSRF is an attack, CSP restricts what a page may load, and HSTS forces HTTPS.
